posts.body_html:
Thanks waxy. Such a stimulating thread. 
John on the other forum mentioned something that I had been thinking about: that form, not varietal, status should be accorded in cases where a single gene accounts for the distinguishing characteristic in a taxon. This thought pretty much opens Pandora's Box, and I therefore humbly submit the following rant:
Flava varieties should be demoted to forms. If "albino" S. purpurea ssp. purpurea is forma heterophylla, why should over-expression of the gene warrant varietal status, as in red-tubed flavas? In the case of "var." rubricorpora there are entire populations exhibiting the red tube gene, which could give the superficial impression of a more significant taxon (and, surely, lay the foundations for future divergence from other populations), but is it really so? And of course even in Florida the red-tubes usually grow with rugelli, while in the Carolinas the special color "varieties" grow in sympatry as a total mixed bag. How could divergence between flava cuprea and flava flava occur under such circumstances? Seems more likely the "different" plants are just due to one gene that is getting shuffled around within the population generation to generation, while the concept that they are any more divergent than that is a misapprehension. 

There are numerous other inconsistencies in the application of taxonomic categories within the genus Sarracenia, with the taxonomic double standard between S. flava and S. purpurea/rosea being the most glaring. It is interesting that no varieties analogous to those described in S. flava have been described in S. purpurea, even though the same color forms exist in both species. To wit: "veinless" purps are not var. maxima, all-red purps are not var. atropurpurea, and purps a la Belly of Blood are not var. rubricorpora, etc. The same features that are the object of so much debate in S. flava have been ignored taxonomically in S. purpurea, being blithely chalked up to the natural variability of the taxon! In my opinion this reflects a very unscientific bias towards the bigger, showier, "sexier" species S. flava. It's like a teacher only paying attention to an attractive student, while neglecting an equally interesting, but fugly, classmate! 

This double standard also occurs in the case of S. rosea, aka "S. purpurea ssp. venosa var. burkii." Despite it's disjunct range and clear differences in trap and flower morphology, some regard this plant as a mere variety of purpurea. C'mon, not even a subspecies? This is certainly inconsistent with the prevailing treatment of S. flava (and, arguably, S. oreophila: I would argue that S. rosea is as distinct from purpurea as oreophila is from flava). It's as if purple pitcher plants aren't "taken seriously" while every shade of S. flava is taxonomically overestimated.

I am, in the course of this little armchair dissertation, taking issue with a portion of the work of Dr. Donald E. Schnell. I have enormous respect for Mr. Schnell, whom I have never met, and his pioneering work with the genus Sarracenia. I do, however, find many of his taxonomic arguments to be less than cogent because of the way they contradict each other. 

Haha thank God this isn't a thread about S. rubra, because honestly folks I don't want to go there!

Thanks rmeyer! I think they can get just as "Hulk Hogan'ed" out in cultivation, and they typically get a lot bigger under greenhouse conditions. I think the limiting factor outdoors here in California is our humidity and night temperatures. If it was warmer at night and a lot more humid during the day, I bet most of the plants would get gigantic.

Despite the environmental limitations, some plants still look like they're on "roids":








Seen a lot of S. psittacinas in the wild, and many giants too, but never anything close to as big as this one. The regular S. psittacina in the front is a specimen sized plant for reference:



On the left is the Caroline Co, VA purp purp, and on the right is a "regular," mature sized S. purp. purp. Marl bog form from Bruce Co, ON:

posts.body_html:
Personally, the biggest purps I have seen have been in Belvidere Vermont. Nothing I have seen in cultivation comes close to the size of the pitchers, or size of the clumps I have seen in that population!

Jan 25, 2014 10:44:39 GMT -5 rmeyer said:
I couldn't help but notice how muscular these plant are....bulky, tough, and bad-ass all in one. I've never seen a cultivated plant look like this. Are these plants in perpetual stress when taken out of their natural habitat or are these plants just that much more mature than the ones we cultivate? Probably both, surely.


As for differences in cultivation vs wild, so far as I have seen for purps in the Northeastern US, the soil mixes are different. Here in the NE, most of the bogs are ombrotrophic live sphagnum bogs, but in cultivation the predominant mix is peat and perlite. In nature I have seen them growing in places dammed by beavers, and other locations where the amount of water is enough to harbor water lilies, utricularia, fish, and many other wildlife. Also they exist alongside cranberries, blueberries, and leatherleaf. The ecology is so complex, it is difficult to completely replicate it in cultivation, and that may be a factor that effects their growth rate.

With that being said many growers, such as Mike and others, have colossal strong plants! Some of it is genetics, and some of it is growing conditions, and some of it is still experience. Mikes kiddie pool set up with many plants in each pool is much closer to nature than my very small "plastic tub/tray" method.

With that said, Mikes last two pictures with the psittacina, and purpurea just goes to show that where a plant comes from (it's genetics) does play a major factor in the plants "strength" and size.

rmeyer and meizzwang This is an interesting discussion! Thanks for bringing it up!

posts.body_html:
MW, for me this reinforces my position in a major way: if there is to be any credibility to variety names being applied within Sarracenia species, then something can't be two things at once. This goes double for red flava specimens and big time for the intensely variable colour within "rubricorpora".

While I'm aware others have a differing perspective, to my mind the elemental questions that arise and need addressing in respect of the variety names "atropurpurea' and "rubricorpora" beyond the simple installation of those names by their original proposer, and beyond simply saying they are all red or not, remain:


1) Is there a significant and thereby isolating geographical demarcation between the red flava populations in NW Florida and the Carolina coastal plain?

2) What is the nominal growth pattern of the distinct populations (clearly they are different i.e, the infamously slow division and low pitcher production of "rubricorpora") and do they set them apart (as readily recognised between concurrent "rubricorpora" and var. rugelii)?

3) Is it fair to say that Liberty Co etc "rubricorpora" colouration can range markedly from yellow hoods with some red veining to hoods fully infused with red? Should that circumstance be recognised simply as the variability of the genetics that present as "rubricorpora" of NW Florida; a distinct reflection of those genetics?

4) Is it the case that this colour range can be seen within stands of "rubricorpora" where those populations are clearly exist on the same genetic foundation?

5) At what point of the pitcher development (pre-opening, just opened, two months down the track etc) do you describe the variety based solely on colour if that is felt necessary? To reiterate, can something be two varieties within the same season or is it in fact a presentation of the population genetics within which it exists?

6) Is it realistic to describe one individual in the centre of otherwise related specimens within the population not so much as an expression of that population's colour range and therefore something notable therein but as something otherwise acknowledged to be native to a location 700 miles away?

7) Is it fair to consider the question of why, within the otherwise accepted geographical stands of "rubricorpora" plants will be described as "atropurpurea" yet no plant in the eastern "atropurpurea" population range is described as "rubricorpora" and no such suggestion has ever existed?

8) Referring to the question of necessity in 5), what lies behind that necessity? Is it the case that we seek to divide the visibly superficial differences to too large a degree without due consideration to other elements?


My responses remain that the reliance on colour alone when it comes to the questions above is unrealistic in considering the distinction between the diverse populations in question and too simplistic in addressing those distinctions. I believe it is well demonstrated that some "rubricorpora" will become fully red having started the growth season as an obvious member of such a population on a number of grounds and, thereby, remain so.

Mike, I firmly believe your Liberty Co. plant is representative of this (as are those I and others have) and goes no way to establishing a relationship between the genetics it derives from and those of "atropurpurea" as found on the Atlantic coast.

posts.body_html:
While color is significant to horticulturalist eyes, it really should not be used to divide/decide taxonomic varieties. Imagine if some said that red Fly Traps were a different variety than the green... or red Nepenthes ampullaria was a different variety than the spotted or green. We're just not understanding the logic. But, for a grower who wants all the different colors it is useful. The field of mixed ornata/rubricorpora/rugelii all intercross with each other, don't they?
There are locational differences between the Carolina stands and Florida because they've been separated for a very long time. When you compare them, they definitely have a different look to them, but they are the same species. Don't understand separating them by color.

posts.body_html:
Resurrecting an old thread here with some observations from the 2015 Searchaganza. I had a number of questions about the all-red S. flava in Santa Rosa and Okaloosa Cos, and so Trey and I were dead-set on finding them on our May and June excursions. We wanted to know: What do they look like when first opening / in the early season? How does their color change over the course of the season? Can we make any observations about their relationship to other color forms both in the same bogs and in other parts of FL? Well we found the plants and I'm happy to be able to share some of our observations here. Pics taken on May 8 and 9 and June 30/31 in Okaloosa Co.

The observation that surprised us most was that contrary to theories put forth by myself and others earlier in this very thread, the Okaloosa Co red flavas are not solid red at the time they open. This had been suggested as a possible criterion to describe them but does not appear to be borne out by observations of wild populations. Visiting a couple different sites that contained "var. atropurpurea" revealed that, on average, plants that will later be solid red look like bronzy ornatas when they first open! 
Taken May 9:

Closer in, same plant

Close-up of pitchers:

Here are shots of the exact same plant, taken on June 30:

Looking downhill, clone in foreground (what a bog!!!!):

Too bad the foreground pitcher is out of focus, but this is the best closeup shot of this clone I got (notice there is a different, less red clone in the background - more on those in another post!):

Going back to May 9, here are some shots of a spectacular group of plants at the same site. The were just opening at the time we visited. Most of the plants that look "red" from this distance are actually heavily veined ornatas that will infuse only later.

Let's have a look at that dark red one - this was the darkest plant in the place on May 9th. As you can see the lid is full of veins, rather than being solid red. This would by definition be a var. rubricorpora, but I say hogwash! 

Another shot of an early season atro in this stand:

Different angle, but same exact patch of plants on June 30:

The ornatas here also darken a lot. May 9:

June 30. Has this plant continued to infuse and turned into a "var. rubricorpora" or a "var. atropurpurea" by today, August 6th? Totally possible!

A few more shots from May:


Nifty psittacina flowers:
